issue_context.title: Developers using JsonSerializer can asynchronously (de)serialize IAsyncEnumerable<T>
issue_context.body:
It would serialize to a JSON array but in a streaming manner. This would be very useful for things like MVC that want to support returning entity framework queries (which implement IAsyncEnumerable) to the response steam without buffering the entire enumeration first (which is what is currently being implemented https://github.com/aspnet/AspNetCore/pull/11118/files).

EDIT @eiriktsarpalis see https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/1570#issuecomment-808496838 for the full API proposal.

review_comments: How long does this take? It should be an OuterLoop test I believe.
It should take 5 seconds, assuming cancellation token support is not broken. Considered adding it to outerloop but it felt like a pretty deterministic test (even though it is longer-running).
OK I wasn't sure how `TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1) was used here.
The name of this method says "Nested" -- what is nested given there is only one enumerator? (same applies to other methods below)
I suppose in this case it means "nested within a POCO", as opposed to the enumerable being root-level.
As a side discussion, should we document a potentially "breaking change" here? The previous behavior of writing "{}" was obviously incorrect, so really we're fixing a bug, not breaking.
Yes, I think we should be proactive about communicating that this is strictly speaking a breaking change.
I assume this fixes the issue today where we don't call Dispose on exceptions (for the non-async case); i.e. previously we only called Dispose on enumerators in the non-exception case.
Yes, even though I just discovered more corner cases in the non-async case. It's becoming involved, so I'm thinking I should address that in a future change to keep this PR focused.
Opened separate issue to track it: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/50851
What is causing the exception here?
Ultimately it originates from a `Stream.ReadAsync()` call that has been passed a cancelled token. Similar to what you would expect in a `DeserializeAsync` call.

> is not null

nit - why this over `!= null`? Would be nice to maintain one pattern throughout the library. Same comment for `is null` elsewhere.

`is not null` and `!= null` are not always identical, e.g. https://sharplab.io/#v2:C4LglgNgPgAgTARgLACgYGYAE9MGFMDeqmJmxpG2cmAYgPZ1kqmHksmUwIBsmARgwiY6ABwCmAJwCGwOhMwBeBQAp6jAB4AaWg0wBPAJSKAfJgBmUiAGcxAbjbtOPfoOHjps+QEIVazFp1GQxNMYAkAVzsHAF9UB04AFkwAWVVdMwYjByJmdhIwM0xlDMYwK0wAOzpgSvCICAMHFhy81uwEAE5lA3tcvNi+zAGWeKwYJIA5NMYSxsGCUibSAqKSzB9a+rm2lraKTu7etuHSAeigA

I don't have a strong opinion about maintaining a consistent way (either form is standard in both C# and .NET libraries), but if we are to force consistency then I would err towards `is` patterns.
Do you know if there are guidelines on when to use either pattern?
Not that I know of, but my understanding is that we try to use `is` patterns for new code.
why not dispose it now? If we could, would we need to keep track of this list?

`IAsyncDisposable` can only be disposed asynchronously, however `Pop()` is called at the converter context which is sync. We need to store it so that it can be disposed properly in the root async context.
